It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing the “noise and tumult” of leaders who “profess to know God, but in works they deny Him,” and I must ask you with a gentle spirit: why do you ask after the nature of hypocrisy in this hour? [13, 1138, 1346, 1407, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by a world where “showmanship” and “gimmicks” have replaced the “spotless purity of truth,” or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the exposing of “whitewashed tombs”? [13, 20, 122, 1143, 1316, 1365, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to offer “spiritual placebos” that “pander for publicity,” we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “vicissitudes of life” by demanding that we “examine everything carefully” within ourselves [11, 28, 116, 1313, 1503, 1515, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the public unfaithfulness of a leader is not an “administrative anomaly” but evidence of “radical depravity” that God uses to “test Israel, whether they will keep the ways of the LORD” [15, 68, 194, 467, 1143, 1532, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Whitewashed Mask of Performative Religion**

**Verse**
“ ‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs which indeed appear beautiful outwardly, but inside are full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness. Even so you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness’ ” (Matthew 23:27–28). [122, 1347, 1472, 1486, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The sources teach that the “most determined enemies” of truth often come from “within the visible church herself,” wearing the “clever camouflage” of religious language to mask a heart that is a “perpetual factory of idols” [2, 1347, 1442, 1486, 1504, Conversation History]. This “performative religion” involves “wearing their religion on their sleeves” to “attract attention and bring honor to themselves” through “showmanship” and “gimmicks,” making their righteousness “mostly cosmetic” [15, 151, 289, 371, 1580, 1614, Conversation History]. Leaders who use the faith as a “cloak for their sin” are “spiritual swindlers” whose “idea of righteousness was mostly cosmetic,” for “the Lord perceives their wickedness” and “knows your hearts” (Luke 16:15) [120, 152, 245, 1111, 1562, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not be deceived” by “outward appearances,” for “every tree is known by its own fruit” and a “spiritual swindler” can maintain a “veneer of charm” while remaining “dead in trespasses” (Luke 6:44; Ephesians 2:1) [6, 91, 164, 214, 223, 1410, 1488, 1502, Conversation History]. Your “sole objective” is to “adorn the doctrine of God” through a life of “joyful obedience,” rather than being “enthralled with this life” or seeking “deliverance” in a “hypocritical” human authority [101, 1032, 1406, 1502, 1670, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Ritual vs. Reality**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, the Pharisees “padded the actual law of God with lots of man-made rules” like “seed counting and gnat straining” to “acquire surplus merit” [168, 171, 308, 336, 408, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this by showing that the Law was never meant to be a “merit system,” but a “mirror” to “reveal the sinful deeds of the flesh” and drive the soul to Christ, for “by the deeds of the law no flesh will be justified in His sight” (Romans 3:20) [234, 239, 300, 316, 900, 1169, 1188, 1403, 1709, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: The Diagnosis of the Proud vs. The Penitent Heart**

**Verse**
“ ‘And the tax collector, standing afar off, would not so much as raise his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me a sinner!” I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted’ ” (Luke 18:13–14). [112, 115, 318, 1271, 1272, 1317, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that “the saved know they are wicked” while “the damned think they are good,” highlighting the “forensic decree” of justification [11, 242, 347, 348, 351, 368, 1601, Conversation History]. The tax collector “confessed his own utter spiritual poverty,” whereas the Pharisee was “smug, self-righteous, [and] contemptuous,” asking God for “absolutely nothing” because he “could think of nothing he needed” [11, 153, 318, 333, 335, 1169, 1403, Conversation History]. This “self-congratulatory” spirit “robbed prayer of its primary purpose: to glorify God,” turning it instead into a “demonstration for people” that “God had no part in” [13, 16, 323, 326, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You must “confess your own utter spiritual poverty,” for “the gospel has nothing to say to people who are satisfied with their own righteousness” [11, 153, 314, 345, 1169, 1403, Conversation History]. Recognize that “the damned believe eternal life is earned” but the “saved know it's a gift” received through the “finished work” of Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9; John 19:30) [11, 351, 666, 839, 1132, 1186, 1406, 1445, 1500, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **context**, the Pharisees added “a long list of petty, man-made restrictions” to the Law to “avoid accidental infractions,” but this “rigid system became a point of immense pride” [196, 197, 308, 336, 408, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our view of status, revealing that “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” and “all have sinned,” meaning that “ritualized ceremonies” and “lineage” do not qualify anyone for the kingdom (Romans 3:22–23; 10:12) [263, 1142, 1201, 1313, 1426, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: Profession of Christ While Denying Him in Works**

**Verse**
“They profess to know God, but in works they deny Him, being abominable, disobedient, and disqualified for every good work” (Titus 1:16). [614, 1407, 1551, 1572, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture reveals that public behavior which “apes the world's fads” while professing faith is often a “double-minded” effort to serve both “God and Mammon” [11, 98, 1324, 1493, 1582, Conversation History]. Leaders who “love the praise of men more than the praise of God” prove they “set their minds on earthly things,” essentially “establishing their own righteousness” while “ignorant of God’s righteousness” (John 12:42–43; Philippians 3:19; Romans 10:3) [303, 316, 410, 1037, 1307, 1416, 1417, Conversation History]. This “no-lordship ideology” creates “carnal Christians” who “live as though He never gave a law to obey” because they are too “enthralled with this life and worldly values” [27, 318, 319, 320, 445, 501, 519, 1502, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Never become so involved in this world” that you treat the “more sure word” as a “platform for your own ego,” for “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31) [11, 13, 34, 51, 121, 130, 862, 1617, 1623, 1684, Conversation History]. You must “discipline your mind” to “hold fast to that which is good” by first “judging yourself,” for “if we would judge ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31) [11, 116, 121, 1406, 1557, 1594, 1684, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Reformed Framework**
The Reformed tradition—summarized by **John Calvin**—asserts that “vanity must first be torn away from us in order that the love of God may reign within us,” for “until our minds are cleansed,” doctrine will have “no effect” [1607, 1638, 1719, Conversation History]. **Jonathan Edwards** further warned of “counterfeit love” that arises from “natural self-love,” where groups “agree one with another in those things wherein they greatly differ from all others” to feed their own “pride” rather than following Christ [654, 661–663, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Final Verdict on Spiritual Fraud**

**Verse**
“ ‘Not everyone who says to Me, “Lord, Lord,” shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven. Many will say to Me in that day, “Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Your name, cast out demons in Your name, and done many wonders in Your name?” And then I will declare to them, “I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness!” ’ ” (Matthew 7:21–23). [138, 148, 251, 263, 1037, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The “apex of human tragedy” is the final judgment of those who “play at religion” while “denying the only Lord God and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 4) [1350, 1397, 1406, 1407, Conversation History]. Public ministry—even “prophesying” or performing “wonders”—is no “proof of genuine conversion” if the heart is “dead in trespasses” and “hostile toward God” [214, 317, 366, 1321, 1410, Conversation History]. The “Lord knows those who are His,” and He will “execute judgment on all” who “speak lies in His name” and “practice lawlessness” (anomia), which is to live “as though He never gave a law to obey” [24, 176, 300, 316, 1137, 1315, 1396, 1450, 1515, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “perfect justice will come” and the “Lord, the righteous Judge,” will “make all things right” at the “consummation of the age” (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Thessalonians 1:10) [24, 94, 109, 1315, 1403, 1408, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. “Trade in your worry for trust,” for “the Word of our God stands forever” while the “furious rage” of unfaithful leaders “will be brought to an end” [11, 13, 21, 94, 121, 1306, 1315, 1408, 1515, 1684, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Revision of Victory**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, “distress” was met with “sackcloth and ashes” as a sign of God’s “fierce anger” against unfaithful leaders like Ahab [372, 858, 875, 876, 881, 1003, 1110, 1140, 1181, 1316, 1457, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “victory,” teaching that the “church militant” conquers not through “carnal weaponry” or “political maneuvering,” but “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony,” for our “citizenship is in heaven” (Revelation 12:11; Philippians 3:20) [13, 21, 32, 92, 1313, 1491, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 300, 324, 361, 405, 414, 444, 591, 1138, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

The apostle John condemned worldliness with equal severity. He wrote, “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15). Did he mean it is a sin to love mountains and flowers or good food and people? Of course not. He is talking about the values and the vices of this world, everything embodied in the world’s pathological and self-destructive enmity toward God: “All that is in the world—the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not of the Father but is of the world” (v. 16).

Why was this particular brand of Judaism so deadly? After all, the Pharisees gave every appearance of being champions of righteousness. In fact, external appearances were what concerned them the most. Their idea of righteousness was mostly cosmetic. They excelled at hiding their own unrighteousness and papering over their secret sins with works of religion—while they declaimed passionately against the more visible sins of others. Far from being careless with respect to the law, they made a great show of obeying the law’s fine points in an exaggerated, ostentatious way (Matt. 23:5). Their use of the law as a cloak for their sin therefore turned the whole purpose of the law on its head. Whereas the law is supposed to reveal sin and show its exceeding sinfulness, they used the law to disguise what was really in their hearts—and they salved their own guilt by self-righteously comparing themselves with others. The subtlety of their error, obscured by the pretense that they were strongly committed to the law of God, is what made their brand of religion so dangerous.

Here is the most abject type of sinner—a tax collector. He is a traitor to his people who has sold out for money. Yet he gains a right standing with God, apart from any religious ritual, absent any kind of self-atonement, and without performing any deeds of merit. Every detail of the doctrine of justification by faith is either expressly set forth, implied, illustrated, or otherwise affirmed in this parable. Not only did Jesus say God accepted the tax collector; He also made it clear that the Pharisee was rejected. “This man went down to his house justified rather than the other” (Luke 18:14). That was stunning. How was such a thing possible?

On an even broader scale, does Jesus’ frequent use of stories constitute a valid argument against the systematic approach to doctrine Christians have historically taken? Do we really even need to analyze Scripture, categorize truth, and attempt to understand biblical doctrine in any kind of logical fashion—or is it okay just to appreciate the stories and embellish them with our own plot twists and real-life endings? In very simple terms: Is Jesus’ own style of teaching actually incompatible with our doctrinal statements, confessions of faith, and systematic approach to theology?

The rest of the New Testament issues similar warnings to anyone who might claim to belong to Christ while persisting in unrepentant sin.22 The first epistle of John is especially clear in this regard. There John wrote, “If we say that we have fellowship with Him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth” (1 John 1:6). And later, “Little children, make sure no one deceives you; the one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as He is righteous; the one who practices sin is of the devil. . . . No one who is born of God practices sin. . . . By this the children of God and the children of the devil are obvious: anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor the one who does not love his brother” (3:7–10). Though many call themselves “Christians,” the true condition of anyone’s heart is ultimately seen in how he lives. As the saying goes, actions speak louder than words. The profession of faith that never evidences itself in righteous behavior is a “dead” faith (James 2:17), being no better than that of the demons (v. 19). This is not to say that true believers never stumble. Certainly they do. Yet the pattern of their lives is one of continual repentance and increasing godliness as they grow in sanctification and Christlikeness.

Thus the apostle Paul could tell the Corinthians that, even in his sacrificial labors on Christ’s behalf, all must be attributed to God’s grace. “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace toward me did not prove vain; but I labored even more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). Similarly, all Christians are called to “work out [their] salvation with fear and trembling” while recognizing that “it is God who is at work in [them], both to will and to work for His good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13). The astonishing reality is that God not only calls us to be dutiful slaves; He also enables us to be faithful to that calling. Moreover, having empowered our service to Him, He then promises to eternally reward us for the faithfulness He has graciously enabled.
